description: I’m Ramzy, a Master’s student in AI/bioinformatics at USTHB, Algiers. During my ASAL research internship I worked on Sentinel-2 forest/built-up classification, satellite super-resolution (Real-ESRGAN vs Stable Diffusion) and gesture recognition for touchless control. I also built an asteroid tracker with NASA’s NeoWs API. Looking for a front-end/UI dev, a space/Earth observation enthusiast and a designer for the demo. Beginners welcome. We’ll aim for a working prototype.
summary: MODIS (2000+) and VIIRS (2012+) detect fires differently, so their records can’t be compared directly. We built a harmonized 2000-to-today hotspot record for Algeria. A curved log-polynomial model estimates monthly VIIRS-equivalent totals from MODIS, HistGradientBoosting places them on a 1 km grid, and the FireLens web app lets users explore the result.
details:
The challenge was to combine MODIS (about 1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012) into one consistent fire history. In overlapping years, VIIRS records about 2.43 fire cell-days for every MODIS cell-day, so simply joining the two records creates a false jump in fire activity in 2012.

Our approach:

  1. Clean the data. We kept only vegetation fires (FIRMS type 0), which removed 56% of Algerian VIIRS cell-days that come from static industrial sources such as gas flares. We also applied confidence filters and excluded sensor-outage months.
  2. Estimate totals. A curved log-quadratic regression on 50 km (0.5°) blocks converts MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent monthly totals.
  3. Place the fires. HistGradientBoosting allocates each block’s total to 1 km cells, using MODIS detections and a 2016–2021 VIIRS burn prior.
  4. Evaluate honestly. We trained on 2016–2021 and tested backward on held-out 2013–2015 VIIRS data. HistGradientBoosting reached 13.9% median error and 1.74 block MAE at 50 km, with much smaller north/south bias than the polynomial or neural network alone. A check on August–December 2012 showed a +1.8% net error against real VIIRS.

Limitations we report openly: the calibration is region-specific (it under-predicts Zambia by 81% when transferred directly), and results vary between years, so outputs should be read with uncertainty bands.

The output is a harmonized catalog that flags estimated rows, plus an interactive web app (FireLens) for exploring the record.
